As a glacier {slo|wly} advances, {ro|cks} frozen into its {ba|se} grind {aga|inst} the {bed|rock} beneath it. This {pro|cess}, known as {abra|sion}, polishes and {scra|tches} the valley floor. At the same time, plucking pulls {lo|ose} blocks of rock away from the walls. Together, these processes {tran|sform} narrow V-shaped river valleys into broad U-shaped troughs. Many of these troughs were carved during the last ice age, when glaciers covered far more land than they do today.

5.5.paragraph: Few geological forces reshape mountain landscapes as dramatically as moving glacial ice. When a valley glacier {adva|nces}, debris {embe|dded} in its base {func|tions} as an abrasive, {gou|ging} striations into the {under|lying} bedrock. {Simulta|neously}, meltwater {refr|eezes} in fractures, {enab|ling} the ice to pluck {ang|ular} blocks from the valley walls. shared.title: Coffeehouses and the Spread of News in Early Modern London
shared.text:
In 1652, the first coffeehouse opened in London, and within a few decades the city had hundreds of them. These establishments sold more than a new drink recently introduced from the Ottoman Empire. For the price of a penny, a customer could buy a cup of coffee and stay for hours, reading the newspapers and pamphlets that owners provided and joining conversations with strangers. Because of this cheap access to information and debate, coffeehouses were sometimes called "penny universities."

Coffeehouses became important centers for the spread of news. Few people could afford to buy every printed publication, so they gathered where papers were shared and often read aloud. Some coffeehouses attracted customers with particular interests. Merchants met in houses where shipping news was posted, while writers and scientists gathered in others. Rumors, political arguments, and reports from abroad passed quickly from one table to the next.

Not everyone welcomed this development. In 1675, King Charles II issued a proclamation ordering coffeehouses to close, partly because he feared they spread false reports and criticism of the government. The public reaction was so strong, however, that the order was withdrawn before it took effect. The episode suggests how central coffeehouses had become to public life.

shared.title: The evidence for continental drift
shared.text: Okay, so today we're looking at one of the big ideas in geology: continental drift. Back in 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents hadn't always been where they are now. He argued that they'd once been joined in a single supercontinent, which we now call Pangaea, and that they'd slowly drifted apart. Now, Wegener didn't just guess. He collected several kinds of evidence. The first is one you've probably noticed yourself. Look at a map, and the east coast of South America fits pretty neatly against the west coast of Africa, almost like puzzle pieces. Second, fossils. Remains of a small reptile called Mesosaurus have been found in both South America and southern Africa. This animal lived in fresh water, so there's really no way it could've swum across an ocean. Third, rocks. Certain mountain belts and rock layers seem to stop at one coastline and then pick up again on the other side of the Atlantic. And fourth, climate clues. Wegener pointed out scratches left by ancient glaciers in places like India and parts of Africa, which are warm today. That makes sense if those lands were once much closer to the South Pole. So, was everyone convinced? Not at all. Most geologists rejected the idea, mainly because Wegener couldn't explain what force could possibly move entire continents. It wasn't until the 1950s and '60s, when scientists studying the ocean floor discovered seafloor spreading, that a mechanism finally appeared. And that work led to the theory of plate tectonics, which we'll get into next time.
